title: Gillick competence and the Fraser guidelines for under-16s
blurb: Assess whether a child under 16 can consent, and apply the five Fraser criteria to contraception and sexual health care.
question: Megan, 15, asks the school nurse for contraception and does not want her parents told. Her boyfriend is 16. Which framework should the nurse use, and what must she check?

teach.body: In Gillick v West Norfolk and Wisbech AHA [1986] AC 112 the House of Lords held that a child under 16 can consent to treatment if they have sufficient maturity and understanding to understand fully what is proposed. This is 'Gillick competence'. In plain English: age alone does not decide; understanding does. Competence is decision-specific, so the same child may be competent for a plaster cast but not for major surgery.
teach.cite: Gillick v West Norfolk and Wisbech AHA [1986] AC 112 (HL)

rows.label: Question
values: Should I give contraception without parents?

teach.caption: Since R (Axon) [2006] the Fraser approach also covers advice and treatment for STIs and termination of pregnancy.

items.label: FLRA 1969 s8 and the MCA instead

items: Consider age, maturity and mental capacity.
Check understanding of the treatment, its purpose and how it will feel.
Check understanding of risks, consequences and alternatives, including doing nothing.
Ask the child to explain their reasoning in their own words.
Check the decision is free from pressure by anyone, including a partner or parent.
Record the assessment for this specific decision.

head: The practitioner is satisfied that...
rows: The young person understands the advice
They cannot be persuaded to tell parents, or let you tell them
They are likely to begin or continue having sex anyway
Without it, physical or mental health is likely to suffer
It is in their best interests to give it without parental consent
teach.caption: All five must be met. Always encourage the young person to involve a parent or trusted adult.

teach.h: Consent and refusal are not mirror images
teach.body: If a Gillick-competent child consents, treatment can proceed even if parents disagree: a parent cannot override that consent. Refusal is different. A competent child's refusal of treatment that may prevent death or severe permanent harm can be overruled by the court. In practice the team seeks senior and legal advice early rather than proceeding on parental consent against a competent child's wishes.

teach.h: Sexual activity: when safeguarding comes first
teach.caption: NICE CG89 1.2.1-1.2.2: pregnancy under 13 means the child has been maltreated; consider sexual abuse at 13 to 15.

teach.body: The nurse sees Megan alone, checks there is no coercion (her boyfriend is a year older, with no power imbalance or gifts described), and applies Fraser: Megan understands the advice, will not involve her parents despite encouragement, will continue having sex, her health would suffer without contraception, and it is in her best interests. All five are met, so the nurse can provide contraception confidentially and records the Fraser assessment.

teach.text: Gillick vs Fraser: Gillick asks whether a child can consent to any treatment. Fraser is the narrower checklist for contraception and sexual health without parental involvement. And under 13, sexual activity always triggers a child protection referral: Fraser does not apply.

items: Gillick: under-16s can consent with sufficient maturity and understanding of what is proposed.
Competence is decision-specific; reassess for each decision and record it.
Fraser: five criteria for contraception and sexual health without parental knowledge (Axon extends to STIs and termination).
A competent child's consent cannot be overridden by parents; refusal of life-saving treatment can be overruled by the court.
Under 13: child protection referral. 13 to 15: assess for abuse and exploitation.

summary: You can now assess Gillick competence for a specific decision and apply all five Fraser criteria for confidential sexual health care. You can also recognise when sexual activity in an under-16 is a child protection matter rather than a Fraser decision.

A.q: Noah, 13, needs a forearm fracture manipulated under sedation. He understands the procedure, risks and alternatives and explains his reasons clearly. His parents are on their way. What determines whether Noah can consent himself?
options: Whether he has reached the age of 14
Whether his parents agree before signing
His maturity and understanding of this decision
Whether a court has formally assessed his capacity to decide
A.why: Under Gillick, a child under 16 can consent if they have sufficient maturity and understanding of what is proposed. It is judged for the specific decision.

whyNot.0: There is no fixed age within under-16s; understanding decides.
whyNot.1: A Gillick-competent child's consent does not need parental agreement.
whyNot.3: Competence is assessed by the clinician, not a court.

A.q: Which situation is the Fraser guidelines' main purpose?
options: Contraception for an under-16 without parental knowledge
Consent by any child under 16 to planned or emergency surgery
Refusal of treatment by a 16 or 17-year-old
Treatment of a child who lacks capacity at 16
A.why: Lord Fraser's criteria guide practitioners giving contraceptive (and, since Axon, wider sexual health) advice or treatment to under-16s without parental consent.

whyNot.1: General consent under 16 is Gillick competence, not Fraser.
whyNot.2: Refusal at 16 or 17 is governed by FLRA s8, the MCA and the courts.
whyNot.3: From 16, lack of capacity is assessed under the Mental Capacity Act 2005.

A.q: Freddie, 12, attends a walk-in centre with a sexually transmitted infection and says he has a girlfriend. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Apply the Fraser criteria and treat him confidentially
Make a child protection referral and treat the infection
Treat him and advise him to tell his parents about the relationship
Delay treatment until a parent can attend with him
A.why: Sexual activity with a child under 13 should always result in a child protection referral. Freddie still needs treatment.

whyNot.0: Fraser does not replace safeguarding for a child under 13.
whyNot.2: Advice to tell parents leaves an under-13's sexual activity unaddressed as a safeguarding matter.
whyNot.3: Delaying treatment harms Freddie; safeguarding and treatment proceed together.

B.q: Priya, 14, was assessed as Gillick competent to consent to a mole removal last month. She now needs major spinal surgery. A colleague says her competence is already established. What is correct?
options: It carries forward until her 16th birthday
It carries forward unless her parents object
It is lost, as major surgery needs parental consent
It must be assessed again for this decision
B.why: Gillick competence is decision-specific. A more complex decision with greater risks needs a fresh assessment.

whyNot.0: Competence does not carry forward across different decisions.
whyNot.1: Parental objection is not what determines competence.
whyNot.2: A competent child can consent to major surgery; the issue is reassessment, not parental consent.

B.q: Ellie, 15, asks for the contraceptive implant. She understands the advice, is sexually active, and her health would suffer without contraception. She says she might be able to tell her mother with help. Which Fraser criterion is not yet met?
options: That she cannot be persuaded to involve her parents
That she understands the advice she has been given
That she is likely to continue having sex
That her physical or mental health is likely to suffer without it
B.why: Fraser requires that the young person cannot be persuaded to tell parents or allow the practitioner to tell them. Ellie is open to involving her mother, so the nurse supports that first.

whyNot.1: She understands the advice, so this criterion is met.
whyNot.2: She is sexually active, so this criterion is met.
whyNot.3: Her health would suffer without it, so this criterion is met.

B.q: Jasmine, 14, is Gillick competent and consents to an appendicectomy. Her father arrives and refuses consent. What should happen?
options: Proceed, as Jasmine's valid consent is enough
Delay surgery until both parents agree to it in writing
Seek a court order before any surgery
Proceed after the mother also signs consent
B.why: A Gillick-competent child's consent is valid and cannot be overridden by a parent.

whyNot.1: Parental agreement is not needed when the child is competent and consents.
whyNot.2: A court is not needed where the competent child consents.

C.q: Sophie, 14, attends a sexual health clinic with a 23-year-old man who answers for her and says she 'definitely wants' the pill. She avoids eye contact. What is the most appropriate first action?
options: Apply the Fraser criteria with both of them present
Prescribe as requested, as she is over 13
See Sophie alone to assess understanding and coercion
Refuse contraception and ask her to return with a parent
C.why: Consent is invalid if the young person is pressured. A large age gap and a controlling companion are warning signs of exploitation, so the nurse sees Sophie alone and follows safeguarding procedures as needed.

whyNot.0: Assessing in front of a possibly coercive adult cannot test free consent.
whyNot.1: Being over 13 does not remove the need to assess competence and coercion.
whyNot.3: Refusing and sending her away loses the chance to protect her.

C.q: Tom, 15, is assessed as Gillick competent and refuses a blood transfusion that doctors believe is needed to prevent his death after trauma. His parents also refuse. What is the best course?
options: Respect the refusal, as he is Gillick competent
Respect the refusal, as both parents also refuse
Give the transfusion on one doctor's best interests view
Seek urgent legal advice for a court decision
C.why: A competent child's refusal of life-saving treatment can be overruled by the court. The team seeks urgent legal advice so the court can decide.

whyNot.0: A child's refusal of life-saving treatment can be overruled by the court.
whyNot.1: Parental refusal does not end the matter where a child's life is at risk.
whyNot.2: Overriding a competent refusal needs the court, not one clinician's view.

C.q: Lily, 15, asks for emergency contraception. She tells the nurse her partner is her 32-year-old swimming coach, who has told her to keep it secret. She seems to understand the advice. What should the nurse do?
options: Provide it under Fraser and keep the disclosure confidential
Provide it and share the concern under safeguarding procedures
Withhold it until her parents have been informed
Provide it and encourage her to report the coach to the police herself
C.why: Lily needs the emergency contraception, but a coach in a position of trust and a demand for secrecy indicate abuse. Child protection concerns are shared even if the young person asks you not to.

whyNot.0: Fraser does not cover keeping child protection concerns confidential.
whyNot.2: Delaying emergency contraception risks harm and does not protect her.
whyNot.3: The professional must share the concern; it cannot be left to Lily.

reteach.title: Can this child decide?
reteach.question: How do Gillick and Fraser fit together?

blocks.body: First ask, 'Can this child understand this decision well enough to make it?' That is Gillick competence, for any treatment. Only for contraception or sexual health without parental involvement do you then ask, 'Are all five Fraser criteria met?' Before either, ask whether there is any sign of abuse or exploitation: under 13 there is a referral every time.

blocks.text: Competence is for this decision only. A competent child's consent stands against parents; a refusal of life-saving treatment can go to court.

explain.body: A child under 16 can consent if they have sufficient maturity and understanding of the proposed treatment, its risks, consequences and alternatives, and can explain their reasoning.

test.q: Which finding most strongly suggests a 12-year-old lacks Gillick competence for a proposed operation?
options: He is younger than most children having this operation
He cannot describe the risks or the alternatives
His parents would prefer to make the decision
He changes his mind after a night to think about it
test.why: Understanding of risks, consequences and alternatives is central to Gillick competence.

whyNot.0: Age alone does not determine competence.
whyNot.2: Parental preference does not decide competence.
whyNot.3: Reconsidering a decision is not evidence of lacking understanding.

explain.body: Understands the advice; cannot be persuaded to involve parents; likely to have sex anyway; health likely to suffer without it; in their best interests. All five are needed.

test.q: Which statement is one of the Fraser criteria?
options: The young person is aged 14 or over
The young person is in a stable relationship
The young person is likely to have sex without it
The young person has already told a teacher or school nurse
test.why: Fraser requires that the young person is likely to begin or continue having sex with or without contraception.

whyNot.0: Fraser sets no minimum age within under-16s.
whyNot.1: Relationship stability is not a criterion.
whyNot.3: Telling a teacher is not a criterion.

explain.body: A Gillick-competent child's consent cannot be overridden by parents. Refusal of treatment that may prevent death or severe permanent harm can be overruled by the court.

test.q: A Gillick-competent 15-year-old refuses life-saving chemotherapy. Who can overrule the refusal?
options: The treating consultant
The Children's Commissioner
The trust's ethics committee
The High Court
test.why: Refusal of life-saving treatment by a competent child can be overruled by the court under its inherent jurisdiction.

whyNot.0: A clinician cannot overrule a competent refusal alone.
whyNot.1: The Children's Commissioner promotes children's rights but has no power over an individual child's treatment.
whyNot.2: An ethics committee advises but has no legal power to overrule.

explain.body: Sexual activity under 13 always means a child protection referral. At 13 to 15, consider sexual abuse and exploitation: age gaps, gifts, secrecy, people in positions of trust.

test.q: A 12-year-old girl is found to be pregnant. What does NICE CG89 state?
options: Maltreatment should be considered as one possibility
Fraser criteria should be applied before any referral
The pregnancy means the child has been maltreated
Referral depends on the age of the father
test.why: CG89 1.2.1: sexual intercourse with a child under 13 is unlawful, so pregnancy in such a child means she has been maltreated.

whyNot.0: 'Consider' is the 13 to 15 recommendation; under 13 it is certain maltreatment.
whyNot.1: Fraser does not apply to under-13 sexual activity.
whyNot.3: The father's age does not change the position under 13.
